name: Commodore 64
description: Commodore's 8-bit home computer, released in 1982, named for its 64 KB of RAM. Its sprites, smooth scrolling and SID sound chip made it a strong games machine, and its price made it the best-selling single computer model. It stayed in production until 1994.
curiosities: Guinness World Records lists it as the best-selling single computer model.
SID designer Bob Yannes later co-founded the synthesizer maker Ensoniq.
Its 1541 disk drive has its own 6502 processor and can run code independently of the computer.
Music written for its SID chip is still composed today, and the High Voltage SID Collection gathers tens of thousands of tunes.
It was announced at the Consumer Electronics Show in January 1982.
Its name comes from its 64 KB of RAM, a lot for a home computer of its price.
Its VIC-II graphics chip can show eight hardware sprites at once.
Commodore's founder Jack Tramiel wanted computers "for the masses, not the classes".
Many games loaded from cassette on the Datasette, which could take several minutes.
Retro Games revived it as the THEC64 Mini in 2018 and the full-size THEC64 in 2019.
story: Commodore's engineers built two chips, the VIC-II for graphics and Bob Yannes's SID for sound, then wrapped them in a computer: the Commodore 64 launched in 1982 at a price below its rivals.

Jack Tramiel's price cuts made it the best-selling home computer of its time. Its SID chip gave it music no rival could match, and it had thousands of games, from Impossible Mission to Paradroid and The Last Ninja.
Estimates put its sales between 12 and 17 million. It was sold until 1994, and the demoscene and chiptune music still use it.
